anchor_comparisons.comparison: The L1 mine exposes a small 3D pile whose direct extraction problem is governed by depth-sorted ray hits, visible blockers, one lava/support hazard, and pick durability. The Drawer baseline has no physics or occlusion, but it adds latent visual-rule induction, a choice of four probes from seven cards, feedback recall, and six dependent final filings. It is above this L1 on inference and multi-phase decision burden, while the mine is harder on 3D viewpoint and click-ray control.

evidence.explanation: The approved L1 is simplified and specifies four directly exposed targets with one lava and one support hazard.
The mine UI exposes a rotating isometric canvas, click-to-mine interaction, durability, hazards, and a simplified/full camera surface.
The anchor grader replays rotations, raycast occlusion, material effects, support collapse, inventory, durability, and interaction-source binding.

anchor_comparisons.comparison: The L2 constellation requires moving a cursor until one target shape converges through an active lens, resisting decoy basins and noise, then making one center click. The Drawer baseline instead requires selecting a contrast set, interpreting four oracle responses, and applying the inferred rule to six specimens. The Drawer is materially heavier in discrete reasoning and total decision count, although the constellation has a stronger continuous cursor-observation component.

evidence.explanation: The approved L2 has two decoys, 26 noise stars, an active reveal radius, and one accepted center click.
The anchor generator creates one hidden coordinate target, decoys, noisy stars, and a public cursor-conditioned surface.

The anchor grader checks the one click's distance and binds the expected input source to the selected interaction mode.

anchor_comparisons.comparison: The L3 board continuously updates a momentum-driven ball, with three ordered lamps, walls, wells, collision response, and a settling cup. The Drawer baseline is static between actions and has no comparable physical control or temporal steering, but its hidden XOR rule, probe planning, response interpretation, and sequential filing create a larger symbolic inference burden. These are different difficulty axes; the Drawer is plausibly in the same broad band as L3 without being uniformly harder.

evidence.explanation: The approved L3 specifies three lamps, three walls, three wells, momentum parameters, and the full analog-drag baseline.
The anchor generator constructs ordered targets, hazards, walls, and deterministic physics parameters.
The visible runtime advances physics ticks and changes velocity from continuous tilt, friction, speed limits, and collisions.
The anchor grader deterministically replays every tilt, physics tick, collision, ordered lamp, and cup transition.

anchor_comparisons.comparison: The L4 courier requires a long route through an 18 by 11 warehouse, five face gates in order, and hidden die orientation revealed only initially and at sparse scanners. The Drawer baseline has fewer physical actions and no changing spatial state, but it similarly couples early information gathering to later decisions through feedback, archive recall, and a fixed sequential tray. The two are comparable high-level tasks with different burdens: courier memory and route control versus Drawer visual concept induction and classification.

evidence.explanation: The approved L4 specifies the 18 by 11, five-barrier, four-scanner, one-face-gate configuration.
The anchor's solution search tracks both warehouse position and all die faces while rejecting gate-invalid rolls.
Each visible roll updates position and orientation and can be accepted or rejected by a face gate.
The anchor grader replays the complete roll transcript, orientation, gate order, scanner visibility contract, and final delivery.

anchor_comparisons.comparison: The L5 candy task enumerates routes over boards that change after every valid swap, consumes a refill stream, multiplies cascade scores, and requires an exact total while avoiding licorice. Drawer d5 is less state-coupled because probes change knowledge rather than specimen geometry and final filings do not alter future specimens. It nevertheless has a four-attribute paired relation, eight feedback tests, a 12-card contrast choice, and eight classifications, so it is a plausible L5 inference profile but remains uncertain below Candy on changing-board planning.

evidence.explanation: The approved L5 baseline requires four changing-board swaps, multi-wave cascades, an exact score, and simplified cell interaction.
The anchor resolves matches with gravity/refill and enumerates route continuations over the resulting board.
A valid swap mutates the board, consumes refill, applies successive waves, changes score, and changes later available actions.
The anchor grader replays the changing swap/cascade state and requires exact move count, score, wave, and forbidden-candy outcomes.

visible_baseline_solution: At d4/full, a screenshot-only agent must inspect the seven visible specimen cards and compare six rendered binary features despite card rotation, scale, palette, paper, and asymmetry variation. It must find a four-card contrast set whose visible variation isolates two rule axes and covers the four binary combinations, drag those four cards into the calibration slot, and read each FILE/RETURN response. The one-record archive shows one stored specimen at a time, so the agent may need to navigate and remember the four responses. The responses identify the hidden XOR-style relation among two of five candidate properties; the agent then opens the tray only after exactly four tests, sees one final specimen at a time, drags each of the six in displayed order to FILE or RETURN, and certifies. Success requires the exact probe order and returned outcomes, valid full drag start/end geometry and travel, the prescribed final order, every correct drawer choice, and a completed certification. There is no need to infer a private answer map from the visible task; the normal path uses only rendered card geometry and returned feedback.

baseline_judgment.rationale: The source supports keeping d4 as a hard, L4-band configuration. It is clearly above the approved L1 mine and L2 constellation in latent-rule inference and dependent decision count, and it is comparable to the approved L4 Blind Dice Courier in the way early observations constrain a later sequential task. It is below the approved L5 Candy Cascade on changing-state search and control, but d4's multi-card concept induction, active probe selection, feedback use, and exact full-drag filing are substantial independent burdens. The comparison is cross-axis rather than a claim that one task dominates every dimension; source evidence does not justify relabeling the baseline.

evidence.explanation: The current profile is explicitly the five-property, four-probe, seven-candidate, six-final XOR configuration with nuisance strength 0.5.
The generator requires a visible contrast plan and defines rule hypotheses and final vectors that can be decoded from probe geometry and returned outcomes.
Visible inference filters rule hypotheses using the observed responses and requires every final prediction to be invariant.
The UI exposes a one-record archive during calibration and only one final specimen at a time after the seal is opened.
The grader binds the mode, replays probes and exact final order, validates full gestures, and requires all six correct filings.

uncertainties: No human or computer-use-agent calibration was available, so the absolute L4 placement remains a source-based judgment.
The static inference burden and the anchors' physical or temporal burdens are not directly commensurable.
The current task contains a conflicting at-most instruction described in finding F1; the level judgment assumes the implemented exact-probe contract is the intended one.

findings.claim: The profile and base-task natural-language instructions say to use "at most" the calibration-test budget, but the visible UI and grader require exactly that many tests.
findings.causal_explanation: The browser opens the final tray only when tested.length equals probeBudget, and the grader rejects an early open and requires tested count to equal the configured probe_count for a pass. A screenshot-only player who follows the literal at-most wording and uses fewer probes cannot complete the task, even though the profile summaries describe a fixed number of tests.

evidence.explanation: Every profile's natural_language says "at most" its calibration count while the summaries and parameters specify fixed counts.
The base task description says four tests, but its natural-language instruction says "at most four".
The cabinet's ready state and BREAK SEAL control are tied to the exact probe budget.
openFinal returns unless the number of tested records equals probeBudget exactly.
The replay rejects opening before the exact probe count.
Passing requires tested count to equal probe_count.

findings.recommended_action: If the exact-count mechanic is intended, change every profile and base-task instruction from "at most" to "exactly" or "use all N". If at-most is intended, change the UI and grader contract together; do not leave the mismatch.

concise_summary: Keep the current d4/full level assignment and the source-supported relative ordering, but revise the profile/task wording so the stated calibration budget matches the exact-count UI and grader contract. The ten configurations preserve the intended world and success problem across simplified/full input surfaces; absolute difficulty remains uncalibrated.
limitations: This is source analysis only; no human calibration or computer-use-agent measurement was available.
No browser, generation sweep, grader run, export check, or other runtime check was performed; those checks belong to the parent.
No historical pre-controls implementation or fixed-seed historical fixture was supplied.
Cross-task absolute levels remain uncertain because the anchors emphasize different combinations of visual inference, physical control, temporal state, and route planning.
The assigned solver reads private state and generator helpers, so it was used only as implementation evidence and not as evidence of a normal screenshot-only solution.
